cells.tense: What was handed to you is being handed on, and the shape changes in your hands each time it lands.
cells.ask: Start one small practice someone close to you could copy, and let them see you keep it through a week you would rather skip.
cells.core:
Someone showed you how a thing is done, and you've been the one showing the next person. That's the ordinary shape of it — you carry a way of doing something and it stays alive because you actually use it. What makes this land is that you adjust as you go. You watch what the other person can take, and you give that, and the thing keeps working because it isn't frozen.

Practice is what keeps it in your hands. The repetition is the part nobody sees, and it's the part that makes the passing-on real. So when you hand it over next, notice that you've been holding it steady on purpose — and that sometimes the steady hand needs a small adjustment. Let the give-and-take be visible. Keep it going, and keep the version alive that the next person can actually hold.
cells.sheetLine: What you carry stays alive because you practice it and pass it on.
cells.verb: CARRYING WHAT IS WORTH KEEPING INTO THE NEXT HANDS
cells.place: AT THE SMALL BENCH WHERE SKILL IS REPEATED INTO THE BODY

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead there is a version of this where everyone does it right, and you are already living back from it.
cells.ask: Pick one rule you hold over other people and let it stand unenforced for a week — keep the practice, drop the insistence.
cells.core:
You're defending something worth keeping, and the defense has gotten ahead of the thing itself. The way you do it has hardened into the only way, and you can feel yourself correcting people who haven't asked. There's a future in your head where the practice is finally safe from being done wrong. You're bracing for it now, and the bracing is costing you the people you wanted to share this with.

What holds this together is focus on the doing — the private repetition that built the skill, not the enforcement of it. When you next catch yourself demanding the form, let it be a small thing you release. Practicing it yourself is the steady part. That's the part that survives contact with other people, and the rest can loosen without losing the thing you're trying to keep.
cells.sheetLine: You're defending the form harder than you're keeping the practice.
cells.verb: CARRYING WHAT IS WORTH KEEPING INTO THE NEXT HANDS
cells.place: AT THE SMALL BENCH WHERE SKILL IS REPEATED INTO THE BODY

cells.tense: There was a place where this was passed to you, and you are still standing on the far side of that door.
cells.ask: Choose one old practice you abandoned and do it once this week alone, for twenty minutes, and write what changed in your hands.
cells.core:
You learned something worth using and then stopped using it, and now each person you meet starts from nothing, including you. It looks like independence, but it's really that the shared thing isn't there. You do your own thing, well enough, and it doesn't connect to anyone else doing theirs.

What you need now is the pattern under the specifics — how a thing works when you stop needing a particular teacher to show it. Patterns show up on their own once you look beneath the surface. Practice one small piece of the old thing alone, without needing it to belong to anything larger yet. Your hands remember what the room forgot. What you build up by yourself can later be handed on; it just needs to start moving through you again first.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped practicing the thing you were handed, and it went quiet.
cells.verb: CARRYING WHAT IS WORTH KEEPING INTO THE NEXT HANDS
cells.place: AT THE SMALL BENCH WHERE SKILL IS REPEATED INTO THE BODY

cells.tense: You are already the one people copy from, and you call it just how you work.
cells.ask: Write down three things you do by habit and that someone watches, then say out loud to one person that you do them on purpose.
cells.core:
People are taking things from you — how you do your work, how you hold a standard, how you keep a practice — and you file all of that under just getting through the week. The teaching is happening anyway. You just keep your name off it. That's the whole gap: what you already do well is coming through, and you haven't let yourself own the shaping of it.

Nothing has to be rebuilt. Look at what you actually do in the quiet hours and notice that someone else has learned it from watching you. Then say one part of that out loud as something you chose, not something that happens to you. That's the adjustment — that same steady keeping, now with your name on it. And it doesn't demand anything of anyone else.
cells.sheetLine: You're already teaching people by habit. Say one part of it was chosen.
cells.verb: CARRYING WHAT IS WORTH KEEPING INTO THE NEXT HANDS
cells.place: AT THE SMALL BENCH WHERE SKILL IS REPEATED INTO THE BODY
